strengths: The paper targets an important and well-motivated failure mode of robot video world models: exposure bias and rapid degradation under autoregressive self-conditioning. The proposed post-training protocol is directly aligned with this deployment regime rather than only improving teacher-forced prediction.

The method is technically coherent: adapting contrastive RL-style diffusion post-training to an x0-prediction/EDM parameterization, branching multiple candidates from a shared autoregressive prefix, and using group-normalized rewards is a plausible and useful extension of recent diffusion alignment methods to robot world models.

The empirical results on DROID are consistently positive. The method improves over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline on full-frame metrics, object/robot-masked metrics, temporal degradation curves, and a blind human preference study, suggesting the gains are not merely background reconstruction artifacts.

The paper includes useful ablations covering reward choice, prefix sampling, group size, prediction horizon, KL regularization, and EMA choices. The masked object/robot evaluation is a good addition because it better probes task-relevant visual fidelity than whole-frame metrics alone.

The manuscript is generally clear, with a well-structured explanation of the closed-loop gap, the training protocol, and the reward construction. The appendix provides enough algorithmic detail to understand the implementation at a high level.
weaknesses: The central claims about reliable robot simulation and policy evaluation are stronger than the evidence. Most evaluation is still visual similarity to held-out DROID trajectories under known actions, while the actual WM-to-real policy-evaluation study is small: only 3 tasks, 3 policies, 5 real rollouts per task-policy pair, and 11 simulated rollouts. This is useful but not yet a convincing demonstration that the model is a reliable virtual environment.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to DiffusionNFT/contrastive diffusion RL and the contemporaneous WorldCompass-style prefix-rollout idea acknowledged in the related work. The paper’s main new pieces are the x0 adaptation, randomized prefix sampling, and multi-view reward engineering; these are valuable, but the conceptual leap is moderate.

Several ablations weaken the case for the chosen design. For example, in Table 6, “Best of 2” outperforms the selected “Best of 5” configuration across all reported metrics, and Table 5 shows very small differences between prefix strategies. Some claimed design choices appear motivated by stability/efficiency rather than by the presented quantitative evidence.

The evaluation lacks important reproducibility and statistical detail: validation set size, number of evaluated trajectories, confidence intervals or variance over random seeds, and sensitivity to sampling randomness are not clearly reported for the main metrics. The human study has only 8 expert raters from an in-house platform, with self-selection of videos to rate, which may introduce bias despite randomizing A/B positions.

The reward is computed against ground-truth future videos from the same dataset distribution, so the post-training procedure is not obviously applicable when ground-truth futures are unavailable or when evaluating novel policies far off the dataset manifold. This limits the broader applicability of the approach and should be discussed more explicitly.

The method is computationally expensive, requiring K=16 candidate rollouts and multi-view perceptual scoring during post-training on 8 H200 GPUs for 3 days. The paper notes this limitation but does not provide enough analysis of the quality/compute trade-off or whether similar gains hold under more modest budgets.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: exposure bias and compounding degradation in autoregressive robot video world models. The framing is relevant to computer vision and robotics, and the motivation for post-training on self-generated rollouts is clear.

The proposed training protocol is coherent at a high level: branching multiple candidate futures from a shared autoregressive prefix is a reasonable adaptation of group-relative preference/RL training to video world models.

The empirical evaluation includes several useful dimensions beyond full-frame metrics, including wrist-camera results, object/robot-masked metrics, temporal degradation plots, ablations, qualitative examples, and a human preference study.

The reported improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are consistent across SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS, especially for the wrist view and masked dynamic regions, suggesting the method may improve rollout fidelity rather than only preserving static backgrounds.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. The core optimization is largely an adaptation of DiffusionNFT/contrastive diffusion post-training, and the paper itself notes a very closely related contemporary work, WorldCompass, using a similar RL post-training/prefix-rollout paradigm. The differences, such as randomized prefix length and x0 parameterization, feel incremental relative to the strength of the claims.

The experimental evidence is not yet strong enough for the claimed state of the art. The main comparisons are mostly against Ctrl-World and previously reported numbers for WPE/IRASim; wrist-camera comparisons are only shown for Ctrl-World. There is no comparison to simpler and highly relevant baselines such as supervised fine-tuning on self-generated/noisy histories, scheduled sampling, DAgger-style data aggregation, reward-weighted regression, or directly training with perturbed histories.

Several ablations undermine the chosen configuration. In Table 6, variants such as group size 16 with no best-of-N and best-of-2 outperform the reported “Ours” setting on nearly every metric, and Table 11 also reports better metrics with a policy EMA/no-EMA alternative than the main model. This makes the method selection and the stated conclusions about design choices appear under-justified.

The human study has serious methodological concerns. It is in-house with only 8 expert participants, participants were allowed to choose which videos to rate, and the paper reports 174 vs. 43 preferences without a clear random sampling protocol. This self-selection can strongly bias the result. The reported confidence interval of [72%, 100%] also appears suspicious for 174/217 wins.

The theoretical section is overclaimed. The derivation depends on strong idealized assumptions, including treating the normalized visual reward as an optimality probability and assuming unlimited capacity/posterior-mean behavior of the reference model. This does not establish the practical convergence guarantees implied in the abstract, nor does it convincingly justify the specific finite-capacity LoRA post-training procedure.

The evaluation is mostly based on visual similarity to held-out dataset futures under known action sequences. This is useful but does not demonstrate that the resulting world model is a reliable simulator for planning or policy improvement. The policy-evaluation appendix is very small, with only three tasks, three policies, five real rollouts per policy, and the world model still systematically overestimates task progress.

Important reproducibility details are incomplete or ambiguous. It is unclear exactly which split is used for post-training versus evaluation, how many validation trajectories are evaluated, whether all baselines use identical preprocessing and inference settings, and whether code/checkpoints/videos will be released. Since the reward uses ground-truth future frames, strict train/validation separation is especially important.

The paper’s writing is generally understandable but has many formatting and polish issues, including missing spaces, typographical errors, and some overconfident phrasing. These do not by themselves determine the decision, but they contribute to an impression that the submission is not fully mature.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: exposure bias and compounding degradation in autoregressive robot video world models. The motivation is clear, and the proposed closed-loop RL post-training protocol is well aligned with the failure mode being addressed.

The method is technically coherent: branching multiple continuations from a shared generated prefix is a natural adaptation of group-relative diffusion RL to autoregressive video, and the x0-prediction derivation is carefully presented with a clear connection to the prior DiffusionNFT objective.

Empirical results are convincing within the chosen setting. The method improves over Ctrl-World and other baselines on DROID across SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS, with particularly meaningful gains on wrist-view and masked object/robot regions where task-relevant dynamics matter most.

The paper provides useful supporting evidence beyond full-frame metrics, including masked object/robot evaluations, temporal degradation curves, ablations over reward design and rollout protocol, and a blind human preference study showing strong preference for the proposed model.

The writing is generally clear and well organized. The figures and training algorithm make the method easy to follow, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges computational cost and the absence of explicit physical/geometric constraints.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is somewhat narrow. The main results are on one base model family and one dataset/split, so it is not yet clear how well the approach transfers to other robot datasets, embodiments, camera setups, or stronger future world-model backbones.

The reward uses LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR, and the primary quantitative evaluation uses the same family of visual fidelity metrics. Masked metrics and human preference help, but the paper would be stronger with more task-level validation in the main experiments, especially showing that improved rollouts materially improve policy ranking, planning, or policy learning.

The human preference study is encouraging but not fully independent: it is in-house, uses 8 expert raters, and allows users to choose which videos to rate. This may introduce selection or familiarity biases, despite the strong reported preference margin.

The method is computationally expensive: K=16 candidate continuations, autoregressive prefix generation, and 8 H200 GPUs for 3 days make the approach less accessible. The paper discusses this, but efficiency/scaling tradeoffs are not deeply analyzed.

Some ablations weaken the case for particular design choices. For example, several alternatives in the appendix are very close or occasionally better than the selected configuration, suggesting that the precise protocol is not always clearly justified by the reported numbers.

The theoretical analysis is useful but relies on idealized assumptions such as unlimited data/capacity and reward-as-optimality modeling. It supports the direction of the objective, but should not be overread as a guarantee for the practical finite-sample RL post-training procedure.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: diffusion robot world models often look good in short teacher-forced clips but degrade badly under autoregressive self-conditioning. The proposed post-training protocol directly addresses this deployment mismatch.

The method is technically plausible and well matched to the problem: branching multiple continuations from a shared generated prefix gives a meaningful group-relative comparison structure for autoregressive video, and the multi-view clip-level reward is simple, dense, and scalable.

The empirical package is stronger than usual for this topic. The paper reports full-frame DROID rollout metrics, object- and robot-masked metrics, temporal degradation curves, human preference results, generalization to Bridge and RT-1, and small real-robot policy evaluation/improvement studies.

Results are convincing on the main visual-fidelity claim: compared with the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline, the method improves DROID external-camera SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS and wrist-camera metrics, with particularly relevant gains on masked object/robot regions.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful implementation details and ablations, including learning rate, reward components, prefix strategy, group size/filtering, horizon, view weighting, KL, and EMA choices.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than high. Much of the conceptual machinery is inherited from contrastive RL/post-training for diffusion models and from closely related long-horizon world-model post-training ideas such as WorldCompass/Self-Forcing-style approaches. The paper’s main novelty is a solid adaptation to multi-view robot video world models rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The theoretical section relies on idealized assumptions such as unlimited capacity, reward-as-optimality probability, and a reference model equal to the posterior mean; this does not justify phrasing such as convergence guarantees carrying over exactly in the practical training regime.

The strongest task-level claims are supported only by small-scale evidence. The policy-evaluation study uses three tasks and three policies with few real rollouts, and the policy-improvement result uses 5 trials per block. These are promising but not enough to establish the model as a reliable simulator for policy optimization.

Ablations are informative but undercut some design-choice claims. Several differences are very small and reported without variance or statistical testing, and some non-default settings appear better than the chosen configuration, making it hard to tell which components are essential versus incidental.

The evaluation depends heavily on reference-based perceptual rewards and metrics against held-out ground truth trajectories. This is appropriate for the stated setting, but it limits conclusions about physical correctness, counterfactual action generalization, and use in settings without known future trajectories.

The human study is useful but not definitive: it is in-house, small, and uses expert raters who could choose which videos to rate. The reported confidence interval also appears questionable for 174 wins out of 217 comparisons, so the statistical presentation should be checked.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper provides many hyperparameters, but it is not clear whether code, checkpoints, exact validation split/sample counts, segmentation details for masked metrics, and human-study materials will be released; the method also requires substantial compute for post-training.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem for action-conditioned robot world models: autoregressive rollout degradation under self-conditioned histories. The motivation is clear and relevant to robotic simulation, policy evaluation, and long-horizon video prediction.

The proposed training protocol is practically sensible: branch multiple candidate futures from a shared generated prefix, score them with visual rewards, and update only LoRA adapters plus the action encoder. This is a reasonable adaptation of preference/RL-style diffusion post-training to multi-view robot videos.

The manuscript reports improvements over Ctrl-World on DROID rollout metrics, including external and wrist camera LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR, masked object/robot metrics, and a human preference study. The qualitative examples and temporal metric plots support the claim that the baseline suffers visible degradation and that the proposed model can reduce it.

The paper includes useful implementation details and several ablations, and it explicitly discusses computational overhead and the limitation that the current rewards are visual rather than physical/geometric.
weaknesses: The main novelty appears limited. The core idea closely follows recent contrastive RL/post-training for diffusion models and a very similar contemporary world-model RL setting. The claimed contribution is mostly an adaptation to Ctrl-World's x0-prediction parameterization plus a prefix-branching protocol; this feels incremental for ECCV unless backed by especially strong evidence.

The theoretical contribution is overstated. The paper claims convergence guarantees carry over exactly, but the appendix essentially derives an optimal predictor under unlimited data/model capacity and strong distributional assumptions. It does not convincingly establish practical convergence or address the nonstationary autoregressive setting, LoRA-constrained optimization, reward clipping/normalization, best-of filtering, or EMA/KL modifications used in training.

The experimental evidence is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. The primary evaluation optimizes and evaluates on largely the same perceptual metrics (LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR), so the improvements may partly reflect reward-metric alignment rather than better world modeling. Physical plausibility, contact consistency, and action-conditioned causal correctness remain weakly evaluated.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and potentially uneven. Several baseline numbers are copied from prior work, some are reproduced, and wrist-camera results are only shown for Ctrl-World. It is unclear whether all baselines use identical splits, action inputs, rollout horizons, preprocessing, and evaluation code. Stronger direct comparisons to self-forcing/rolling-forcing-style methods or other closed-loop adaptation baselines are needed.

Several ablations undermine rather than support the chosen method. For example, group size 4, no best-of-N, best-of-2, and EMA variants sometimes outperform the reported default, while differences for reward design, prefix strategy, KL, EMA, horizon, and view weighting are often tiny. This suggests the method is sensitive, under-tuned, or that many design claims are not empirically well supported.

The human preference study has important methodological weaknesses: only 8 in-house expert users, users were allowed to choose which videos to rate, and the study is compared only against the baseline. This introduces selection and familiarity biases and makes the 80% preference rate less convincing than the paper presents.

The robotics utility claims are weakly supported. The world-model-to-real correlation experiment uses only three tasks, three policies, and five real rollouts per policy; the reported correlation gain over the baseline is small. The policy improvement experiment is even more under-specified and appears to use very few real trials, making the claimed downstream impact tentative.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper reports substantial compute requirements but lacks sufficient detail on data splits, sample counts for validation metrics, random seeds, statistical uncertainty for most metrics, and whether code/models/videos will be released. The reported paired 98% win rate and p-values are hard to assess without these details.

The conclusion overclaims that the method transforms video generators into reliable persistent robot simulators. The presented evidence shows improved visual fidelity on benchmark rollouts, not reliable simulation of dynamics, contacts, success conditions, or policy outcomes. This mismatch between evidence and claims is a major reason the paper does not make a convincing acceptance case.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and concrete failure mode of action-conditioned robot video world models: autoregressive exposure bias and rapid long-horizon rollout degradation. This is a timely problem for using world models as simulators for policy evaluation and improvement.

The proposed method is technically sensible: branching multiple candidate continuations from a shared autoregressive history state is a natural adaptation of group-relative diffusion post-training to closed-loop video prediction, and the paper gives a clear explanation of why this grouping is needed.

Empirical results are strong on the main DROID evaluation. The method improves over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline on all reported full-frame metrics for 14-step rollouts, with especially meaningful gains on wrist-camera quality and masked object/robot regions.

The evaluation is broader than a single table: it includes temporal degradation curves, paired per-sample comparisons, qualitative rollouts, object- and robot-centric masked metrics, a human preference study, ablations, and additional Bridge/RT-1 generalization experiments.

The paper is clearly written overall, with useful implementation details, training cost, hyperparameters, and appendix ablations that make the main design choices relatively easy to understand and reproduce.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than large. Much of the method builds on DiffusionNFT-style reward-contrasted denoising and Ctrl-World; the main adaptation to x0 prediction and autoregressive branching is useful, but the theoretical contribution appears fairly close to an existing framework under different parameterization assumptions.

The main reward is based on reference visual similarity metrics against ground-truth futures. This is effective for dataset-conditioned rollout fidelity, but it does not directly establish physical correctness, causal validity, or usefulness in open-ended policy optimization settings. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but some simulator-related claims feel stronger than the evidence supports.

The real-robot policy evaluation and improvement evidence is promising but small scale: only three tasks and three policies for correlation, and only 5 trials per block in the policy-improvement experiment. These results should be viewed as suggestive rather than definitive evidence that the world model improves downstream robot learning.

Some baseline comparisons are imperfect. WPE and IRASim numbers are partly taken from prior work, wrist-camera comparisons are mainly against reproduced Ctrl-World, and the Self-Forcing-style baseline is an approximation rather than a direct application of the original method. This does not invalidate the gains, but weakens the strength of the SOTA claim.

The human study supports the qualitative claim but has limitations: it uses 8 in-house expert raters, allows users to choose which videos to rate, and the confidence interval reporting appears unusually broad for 174 wins versus 43 losses. More detail on sampling, independence, and possible selection bias would strengthen this evidence.

Several ablations show that the submitted default is not always the best-performing configuration, especially for best-of-N filtering and EMA variants. The authors justify this as a conservative/efficiency choice, but it makes the exact recipe and claimed optimal design less clean.
